**The 66 megamat pairs keep their own matrix.** The statistics on the 12 odors shared with the megamat panel are computed against the megamat ORN recordings' own distances: correlations within each of the 9 flies across the glomeruli imaged in it (38 in all), averaged over flies. These are [the structure beyond the ORN input](#fn-orn-residual), the ρ's with the ORNs in [the comparison with Remy's megamat KC data](#fn-yang-remy) and the ORN distance of [the wiring-sharing scores](#wiring-feature). All 66 pairs are within one panel, so no pair of that matrix is on another scale than the rest, and it was left as it was.

### How "structure beyond the ORN input" is computed {#fn-orn-residual}

1. **Subset odor distances to megamat.** Since Yang's APL16 panel only includes 12 of the 17 odors in Remy's megamat panel (its other 4 odors come from validation2), we subset the ORN / KC / embedded-VCF odor-odor distances down to these 12 odors, leaving us {{data:n_ref_pairs ~ .0f}} pairs of the 120 in Yang's full APL16 panel.
2. **Linear prediction.** For KC odor-odor distances, from one model or the mean over per-recording distances, fit KC distance = a + b × mean ORN distance across the {{data:n_ref_pairs ~ .0f}} pairs by ordinary least squares. The ORN distances of this fit are the megamat ORN recordings' own, one minus the Pearson correlation across the glomeruli imaged in a fly (38 in all), computed within each of the 9 flies and averaged over flies; they are not [the 16-odor matrix of fly-mean responses](#fn-orn-recipe), and its change of 2026-11-13 does not touch them. Each set of KC distances gets its own a and b. For the control flies, b = {{data:ctrl_orn_fit_slope ~ .2f}}, a = {{data:ctrl_orn_fit_intercept ~ .2f}}, and R² = {{data:ctrl_orn_fit_r2 ~ .2f}}.
3. **Residual.** Each pair's KC distance minus the line's prediction. Because a and b are fitted to each set of KC distances, any part of those distances that is a straight-line function of the mean ORN distances goes into the line. That includes a uniform offset, such as a higher overall level of decorrelation, and a uniform stretch. The residual keeps only how individual pairs depart from that line, and by construction it is uncorrelated with the mean ORN distances.
4. **Comparison.** ρ between the residual and either the residual of Remy's wild-type KC soma matrix, computed the same way (structure vs wild-type somata: {{data:ctrl_struct_wt ~ .2f}} for the control flies), or the hyperbolic natural-source distances themselves, including the {{data:n_vcf_filled ~ .0f}} pairs whose raw natural-source value is missing and is filled by the embedding (natural-source alignment: {{data:tnt_vcf ~ .2f}} with APL output blocked (TNT)).

A dependence on the ORN distances that is curved but monotone, as a threshold produces, also leaves a systematic residual, which this statistic counts as structure beyond the ORN input: in the left panel, the within-group pairs with small ORN distances all sit below the line.

![Left: the control flies' KC distances against the mean ORN distances for the 66 megamat pairs, with the least-squares line and each pair's residual (red above the line, blue below). Middle: the control residual against the same residual of the wild-type KC somata. Right: the residual with APL output blocked (TNT) against the natural-source distances; hollow points are the pairs whose natural-source value comes from the embedding.](results/summary_background/orn_residual_example.png)

### How Yang's KC distances compare with Remy's megamat KC data {#fn-yang-remy}

Two of the page's statistics (the structure vs wild-type somata, and the 66-pair residual that the natural-source alignment is computed from) rest on Remy's wild-type megamat KC data: trial-mean responses of KC somata imaged in 18 flies (4 from 2022 and 14 from 2018–19 with partial odor panels), 17 megamat odors at 10^-3, distances as one minus the Pearson correlation across KCs. Yang's APL16 data share 12 of those odors ({{data:n_ref_pairs ~ .0f}} pairs), at the same concentrations, with distances as one minus the cosine similarity across KCs, per recording and averaged.

On those pairs the two labs' wild-type matrices agree at ρ={{data:rho_ctrl_remy_soma ~ .2f}} on odor-odor distances (90 % interval over Yang's recordings {{data:rho_ctrl_remy_soma.lo ~ .2f}} to {{data:rho_ctrl_remy_soma.hi ~ .2f}}; Pearson r {{data:pearson_ctrl_remy_soma ~ .2f}} between the two sets of distances; {{data:rho_ctrl_remy_soma_2022 ~ .2f}} against Remy's 2022 flies alone), against a measurement ceiling of {{data:ctrl_ceiling_66 ~ .2f}} for Yang's control matrix on these pairs; a single control recording agrees with Remy's mean at ρ={{data:ctrl_rec_rho_remy_soma ~ .2f}} and with the mean of the other ten control recordings at {{data:ctrl_rec_rho_loo ~ .2f}}. Remy's KC claws agree less ({{data:rho_ctrl_remy_claw ~ .2f}}). The ranking is what agrees; the levels are on different scales (correlation and cosine distance), with Remy's somata at a mean of {{data:remy_soma_mean_66 ~ .2f}} and Yang's control flies at {{data:ctrl_mean_66 ~ .2f}} on the same pairs.

Remy's wild-type somata sit closer to the ORN input than Yang's control KCs do (ρ on odor-odor distances with the ORNs {{data:rho_remy_soma_orn ~ .2f}} against {{data:rho_ctrl_orn_66 ~ .2f}}; Yang's flies with APL output blocked {{data:rho_tnt_orn_66 ~ .2f}}), and Yang's APL-blocked matrix agrees with Remy's somata as well as the control matrix does ({{data:rho_tnt_remy_soma ~ .2f}} against {{data:rho_ctrl_remy_soma ~ .2f}}): on this panel, Remy's somata are intermediate between Yang's two genotypes in their ORN-likeness. What they share with the control matrix in particular is the part beyond the ORN input: the 66-pair residuals agree at ρ={{data:ctrl_struct_wt ~ .2f}} for the control flies and {{data:tnt_struct_wt ~ .2f}} with APL output blocked, which is why the "structure vs wild-type somata" of a model is read against the control flies' value.

The pairs that differ most between the two wild-type matrices are 2h–eb (far apart in Yang's control flies, among the closer pairs in Remy's somata) and the pairs of ms and t2h with other odors, which Remy's somata place further apart. A separate note (reports/note_yang_remy_agreement.html) has the full tables and figure.

### A KC spike's drive to APL and the integration step {#fn-spike-step}

olfsysm integrates the model in steps of 0.5 ms, and a KC spike lasts one step. In the models whose APL is driven by KC spikes, each spike used to add a fixed amount to APL's input current for that one step, so the drive per spike scaled with the step.

A time-step check of the integrator, at fixed tuned parameters, found that the 70 Hz spike-driven base's APL peak fell from {{numerics_dt_check/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.5:inh_peak_on ~ .1f}} to {{numerics_dt_check/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.25:inh_peak_on ~ .1f}} and {{numerics_dt_check/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125:inh_peak_on ~ .1f}} and its APL-on response rate rose from {{numerics_dt_check/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.5:rate_on ~ .1%}} to {{numerics_dt_check/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.25:rate_on ~ .1%}} and {{numerics_dt_check/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125:rate_on ~ .1%}} as the step went from 0.5 to 0.25 and 0.125 ms, with {{numerics_dt_check/flip_fractions.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.25;condition=on:frac_responses_flipped ~ .0%}} to {{numerics_dt_check/flip_fractions.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125;condition=on:frac_responses_flipped ~ .0%}} of its APL-on responses changing, while the claw-driven base changed {{numerics_dt_check/flip_fractions.csv:base=claw_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.25;condition=on:frac_responses_flipped ~ .0%}} to {{numerics_dt_check/flip_fractions.csv:base=claw_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125;condition=on:frac_responses_flipped ~ .0%}} of its responses.

The spike's drive is now scaled by the ratio of a reference step (0.5 ms) to the step in use, so each spike adds the same charge to APL's input whatever the step, and at 0.5 ms every output is identical to before; no result on this page changed. Re-run with the fix, the same base's APL peak goes from {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.5:inh_peak_on ~ .1f}} to {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.25:inh_peak_on ~ .1f}} and {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125:inh_peak_on ~ .1f}} and its APL-on response rate from {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.5:rate_on ~ .1%}} to {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.25:rate_on ~ .1%}} and {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125:rate_on ~ .1%}}, with {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/flip_fractions.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.25;condition=on:frac_responses_flipped ~ .0%}} to {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/flip_fractions.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125;condition=on:frac_responses_flipped ~ .0%}} of its APL-on responses changing, as few as in the claw-driven base; the remaining changes come from spike times falling on whole steps. The odor-odor distances were unaffected throughout (ρ on odor-odor distances with the 0.5 ms matrices {{numerics_dt_check/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125:rho_on_vs_ref_dt ~ .3f}} before the fix and {{numerics_dt_check_spike_fix/per_dt_stats.csv:base=spike_driven_thr70;dt_ms=0.125:rho_on_vs_ref_dt ~ .3f}} after, at 0.125 ms).

### What "oracle" means on this page {#fn-oracle}

An oracle, here, is a model manipulation that is handed part of the answer. Instead of a circuit rule the fly could implement, the manipulation is given a list of exactly which KCs or which glomeruli to change, read off the KC data or off the model's own output scored against the data, and changes exactly those. Its result is a ceiling: an existence proof that changing those elements would be sufficient, made meaningful by controls that make the same change to random KCs or random glomeruli and show that the identity of the elements is what matters.

It is never a mechanism; the question each oracle leaves behind is what in the circuit could single out those elements. The page uses two oracles, the oracle co-responder suppression and the oracle glomerulus gain, each with a footnote below, and one partial one: the breadth × shared-input APL rule's shared-claw term used glomeruli chosen from the two ester groups themselves, which the panel-general rule was then built to avoid.

The progress plot leaves all of these out (the co-responder suppression, the gain's glomerulus subsets in the decomposition, the block-specific glomerulus set), and with them every model that carries the glomerulus gain at all, whether applied at fixed parameters or held fixed inside a fit (the combined-model fits, the reference model and the operating-point fits included), because the best of them on any statistic would be a selection made with the data in hand: on that plot the best so far is always a model given nothing from the KC data but its fitted parameters. The best-models table, by contrast, shows the gain-carrying fits beside the rest, with the gain named in their headers.

### The oracle co-responder suppression {#fn-oracle-coresponders}

**What was done.** On the claw-dynamics base, with and without the coincidence rule, the model was tuned with APL on and run with APL off, and the co-responders were defined from that APL-off run as the KCs responding to at least one fruity ester (2h, IaA, pa) and to at least one small ester (2-but, eb, ep). The connectome APL→KC weights of those KCs' claws were then multiplied by a factor (4 in the variant this page quotes; 8, and 1000, which leaves APL acting on those KCs alone, were also run), the APL re-tuned to the 5 % response rate, and the model scored with APL on and off like every other variant.

**Why it is an oracle.** The set of KCs to inhibit was chosen by the outcome wanted. The block is the pair-specific separation of the fruity esters from the small esters, and these are exactly the KCs that keep the two groups' representations close; no circuit rule picked them, the model's own output did, read against what the data show.

**The controls.** The same factor on an equal number of random KCs outside the set, and on the co-responders of a different pair of odor groups (the alcohols and the aldehydes); neither produces the block.

**What it established.** Removing exactly those KCs is sufficient for the block at the measured size, with the control flies' excess profile and the best ρ on odor-odor distances of its base, so the mechanisms that followed (the breadth × shared-input rule, KC–KC lateral inhibition) were judged by how much of this suppression they reproduce without being told the set. "The oracle's suppression without the oracle" is the KC–KC term achieving most of the same removal through the connectome's claw-to-claw contacts.

### The oracle glomerulus gain {#fn-oracle-gain}

**What was done.** In the PN→KC wiring, the columns of eight glomeruli (VA7m, DL1 and D for ms; DM1 for B-myr and paa; DP1m and VC1 for euc and -aPine; DC2 and DM5 for 1-8ol) are multiplied by a factor, 1.5 on this page unless a column says 1.25 (2 and 3 were also run in the original experiment), so every claw a KC receives from those glomeruli counts that much more in its summed input: a PN→claw gain, applied before the per-claw threshold. The somatic threshold is then re-tuned to the target response rate and, in the fitted models, the APL scales and the KC–KC scale are fitted with the gain held fixed.

**Why it is an oracle.** The glomeruli were chosen as the ones the five weak-input odors drive most in the lab's ORN data, after those five odors had been identified as the ones the threshold model fails to recruit relative to the KC data. The set therefore encodes which odors the model was known to miss, and the factor 1.5 was set by hand to recruit them, not derived from anything in the model or the anatomy.

**The controls.** The same gain on eight random ORN-driven glomeruli outside the set (it recruits nothing and disorders the code), and the anatomical alternative, each claw weighted by its PN→KC synapse count (it recruits two of the five odors and loses the alignment).

**What it stands for.** Since the identity of the glomeruli carries the effect, not the extra drive, and the calyx anatomy of those glomeruli is ordinary (the substrate check), the gain is read as a proxy for something glomerulus-specific upstream of the calyx: an ORN→PN gain, a release probability the synapse counts do not show, or ORN input the lab's data understate for these odors by about that factor at the PN level; the Hallem-input test supports the last reading for ms and paa.

**Where it lives on.** The gain is a fixed setting of every combined model, of the reference model and of the operating-point fits, and the decomposition and the reduced-set fits ask which of the eight glomeruli it needs (next footnote).

### The oracle glomeruli as a set {#fn-oracle-glomeruli}

The eight glomeruli of the oracle gain (VA7m, DL1, D, DM1, DP1m, VC1, DC2, DM5) are also treated as a set in three later analyses.

- The substrate check compared their representation in the model's calyx wiring (PNs present, boutons, claws per presynaptic site) with the other ORN-driven glomeruli's, to ask whether the hemibrain's calyx anatomy could justify a gain of 1.5 for them; it cannot, the correction the anatomy would justify being centred on 1.
- The decomposition split the gain by glomerulus at the reference model's fitted parameters and found that its structural part, the natural-source alignment, comes from DC2, which is not a weak-odor glomerulus, while the five weak odors are recruited by their own glomeruli and the block needs DM5.
- The reduced-set fits then put DC2 alone, or DC2 with DM5 and DM1, into the joint fit in place of the full set.

In each of these the set is still the oracle's: asking which members it needs does not make the choice of the set less of an oracle, which is why the decomposition's subsets are left out of the progress plot (the best subset per statistic would be a selection made with the data in hand). The open measurement question names the same glomeruli: the ORN responses of the oracle glomeruli to the five weak-input odors at the KC data's concentrations.

### The trial-to-trial noise put into the model, and the pipeline that measures it {#fn-trial-noise}

The noise is per-KC excitability jitter. On each simulated trial every KC's spiking threshold is multiplied by its own random factor, 1 + σ ξ, with ξ a standard normal draw made once per KC and trial and shared by that trial's APL-on and APL-off runs (a factor below 0.01 is clipped to 0.01). σ is calibrated per model so that the model's single-trial same-odor floor, one minus the cosine similarity between two trials of the same odor, matches the control flies' {{data:ctrl_single_trial_floor ~ .2f}}, and the mean threshold is re-tuned so that the per-trial APL-on response rate stays at the deterministic run's.

Thirty such trials, drawn from a seeded generator so that every model gets the same draws, are grouped into ten pseudo-recordings of three and processed as the KC data are: the three trials of a recording are averaged, the cosine distances between odors are taken on those means and averaged over the recordings, and the fruity × small-ester block is the mean isotonic excess of the nine pairs; the grand mean over all thirty trials is reported beside it. "The pipeline" on this page is this procedure, and "the block through the noise" its block. Noise on the PN firing rates was tried first and set aside because it averages out over the response window and cannot reach the data's floors; jitter of each glomerulus's input gain reaches them as the threshold jitter does and is the alternative the trial-to-trial variability experiment kept beside it.

**How this noise compares with the flies'.** Because ξ is drawn once per KC and trial, a KC's threshold is off by the same factor for all odors of a trial: all of the model's trial-to-trial variability is shared between the odors of a trial. In the recordings only part of it is.

The same-repeat gap, the single-trial distance between two odors of different repeats minus that between two odors of the same repeat, is {{data:repeat_gap_ctrl ~ .3f}} in control flies and {{data:repeat_gap_tnt ~ .3f}} with APL output blocked (TNT), and at its matched level the pipeline gives the breadth-2 APL-effect fit {{E81/shared_state.csv:model=C2;condition=both:gap_on ~ .3f}} with APL on and {{E81/shared_state.csv:model=C2;condition=both:gap_off ~ .3f}} with APL off. With the noise re-specified to the flies' shares, a smaller shared jitter plus noise independent between odors, the scores of the populations of wirings read through the pipeline hardly move, and the block of the reference family's fits is cut by less ([the flies' variability across the three repeats](#repeat-structure)).

### The threshold margin of a KC × odor entry {#fn-margin}

For one KC and one odor in a deterministic run, the margin is the factor by which that KC's threshold can be scaled before its response to the odor disappears (for a responder) or appears (for a non-responder), minus one: a margin of +0.2 means the response survives a threshold 20 % higher. It is found by recovering the KC's exact input drive over time from its membrane-voltage trace (the summed claw input after the per-claw knee and the APL inhibition, minus the KC–KC inhibition from the other KCs' spikes in that run) and integrating that drive again with olfsysm's membrane equation at scaled thresholds, every other KC held as in the deterministic run, the scale found by bisection. Because the trial noise multiplies thresholds by 1 + σ ξ, a margin expressed in units of σ gives the probability that the entry flips on a noisy trial with the rest of the network held fixed.

### The margin proxy and the replayed trials {#fn-replay}

The margin proxy predicts what the pipeline would measure (the floors, the per-trial response rates, the odor-odor distances, the block through the noise) from one deterministic run, without simulating the noise. It does so by replaying trials: for each of the pipeline's thirty trials it takes the exact jittered thresholds the pipeline draws for that trial (the same seeded draws, the same re-tuned mean threshold, the same clipping) and integrates every KC's recovered drive at those thresholds; the spike counts per KC and odor that come out are one replayed trial, and the thirty are processed exactly as the pipeline processes its simulated trials.

The one difference from the pipeline is that nothing else in the network reacts to the jitter: each KC's drive carries the KC–KC inhibition from the deterministic run's spikes, not from the other KCs' spikes on that noisy trial. APL is driven by the claws and the PN layer is not jittered in these models, so the KC–KC inhibition is the only feedback the replay leaves out, which is why the proxy reproduces the pipeline exactly for a model without KC–KC inhibition and departs from it in proportion to that inhibition's weight relative to the threshold.

### The network-aware margin proxy {#fn-network-proxy}

The margin proxy holds the other KCs' spikes, and with them each KC's KC–KC inhibition, at the deterministic run's; on a real noisy trial those spikes change too. The network-aware version adds that reaction by iteration: the replayed spikes of all KCs from the first pass are low-pass filtered as olfsysm filters them, each KC's inhibition is recomputed from them through the KC–KC weights, every KC is replayed again at the same jittered thresholds, and the step is repeated. Each pass adds one round of the network responding to the jitter, still without a new simulation.

The iteration is synchronous over whole trials, where olfsysm's integration couples the KCs step by step, so whether the passes converge to the pipeline's trials is the question the experiment asks: if a few passes converge onto the pipeline's numbers, a noise-robustness score cheap enough for a fitting loss exists; if they oscillate, the network's response at that inhibition strength needs the simulation.

### How the calibrated readout of the model's spike counts works {#fn-calibrated-readout}

**What is done.** A model's distance between two odors is a cosine distance across KCs on spike counts (one count per KC and odor, the spikes in the response); the flies' is a cosine distance on z-scored trial means of a nuclear calcium signal, which compresses large responses. The readout replaces each spike count n by n / (n + k) before the model's distances are taken; k, the half-saturation count, is the number of spikes at which the readout reaches half of its maximum of 1.

Zero stays zero and a larger count always reads larger, so which KCs respond (two or more spikes), every response rate and the realism bands are exactly as on raw counts; what changes is how much each responding KC weighs in the cosine. With the current reference model's k of {{E65/key_models.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3;readout=saturating_cal_pr:param ~ .1f}} spikes, a KC that fires 2 spikes reads {{lit:0.16 # n / (n + k) at n = 2 with the reference model's calibrated k, 10.46 spikes (results/E65_spike_count_readout/key_models.csv, readout saturating_cal_pr, column param)}}, one that fires 20 reads {{lit:0.66 # n / (n + k) at n = 20 with the reference model's calibrated k, 10.46 spikes (results/E65_spike_count_readout/key_models.csv, readout saturating_cal_pr, column param)}}, and the model's most active KC with APL on, at {{E65/model_amplitude.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3:max_count_on ~ .0f}} spikes, reads {{lit:0.88 # n / (n + k) at n = 78, the reference model's largest APL-on count, with its calibrated k, 10.46 spikes (results/E65_spike_count_readout/key_models.csv, readout saturating_cal_pr, column param)}}: it weighs {{lit:5.5 # the readout of 78 spikes over the readout of 2 spikes, n / (n + k) with the reference model's calibrated k, 10.46 spikes: 0.882 / 0.160}} times as much as the 2-spike KC, where on raw counts it weighs {{lit:39 # 78 spikes, the reference model's largest APL-on count (results/E65_spike_count_readout/model_amplitude.csv, column max_count_on), over 2 spikes}} times as much.

**How k is set.** k is set for each model separately, on that model's spike counts with APL on, and never on the APL effect.

The quantity matched to the flies is the participation ratio of an odor's response vector, (Σx²)² / (N Σx⁴) over the N KCs' values x: the effective fraction of the KCs that carry the odor's squared response, the quantity a cosine weighs (1 when all KCs carry it equally, 1/N when one KC carries all of it). It is computed on responders only (in a recording, trial means at or below 1 set to 0; in a model, entries under two spikes set to 0, for this statistic alone) and averaged over the 16 odors and, in the flies, over the {{data:n_recordings_ctrl ~ .0f}} control recordings.

The control flies' value is {{data:ctrl_participation_ratio_resp ~ .1%}} ({{data:tnt_participation_ratio_resp ~ .1%}} with APL output blocked (TNT)); the current reference model's raw counts with APL on give {{E65/model_amplitude.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3:participation_ratio_resp_on ~ .1%}}, a response more concentrated than the flies'. A small k evens out the responders and raises the ratio, a large k leaves the counts almost as they are, and k is the value at which the readout of the model's APL-on counts has the control flies' ratio, found by bisection on log k between 0.001 and 1000 spikes (when no k in that range reaches it, the nearer end is used, as for {{lit:47 # results/E65_spike_count_readout/by_variant_readout.csv: rows with readout saturating_cal_pr whose at_bound is true}} of the {{E65/readout_summary.csv:readout=saturating_cal_pr:n_variants ~ .0f}} saved models).

The same k is then applied to the model's APL-off counts, every count read, single spikes included. Nothing from the flies with APL output blocked (TNT) and nothing about the effect enters the calibration, so the APL-off distances and the per-pair APL effect remain predictions.

The calibration gives {{E65/key_models.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3;readout=saturating_cal_pr:param ~ .1f}} spikes for the current reference model, {{E65/key_models.csv:folder=E10_joint_fit;tag=k2;readout=saturating_cal_pr:param ~ .1f}} for the first joint fit and between {{lit:4.5 and 15 # results/E65_spike_count_readout/key_models.csv, readout saturating_cal_pr, column param: 4.52 to 14.94 over the nine key models (E65_spike_count_readout.md)}} spikes across the models examined most closely, far from both a k below one spike, which would count every firing KC alike, and a k above the largest counts, which would leave the counts as they are. Fits of the main target that carry the readout in their loss set k again at every evaluation, on that evaluation's APL-on counts.

**The alternatives, and what the readout is not.** Other ways of fixing the compression without reference to the APL effect were run beside this one: a power-law readout, n raised to a power below 1, calibrated in the same way; the saturating readout calibrated instead to the share of an odor's squared response held by the top 1 % of KCs among the control flies' responders ({{data:ctrl_top1_share_resp ~ .0%}}), to the coefficient of variation (standard deviation over mean) of their responders' amplitudes ({{data:ctrl_resp_amp_cv ~ .2f}}) or to their participation ratio on all values, sub-threshold ones included ({{data:ctrl_participation_ratio_all ~ .1%}}); and a map that sends the model's APL-on counts, rank for rank, onto the control flies' pooled responder amplitudes.

They agree: for the current reference model the APL-effect loss is between {{E65/key_models.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3;readout=power_cal_pr:apl_effect_rmse ~ .3f}} and {{E65/key_models.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3;readout=saturating_cal_pr_all:apl_effect_rmse ~ .3f}} under these alternatives, against {{E65/key_models.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3;readout=saturating_cal_pr:apl_effect_rmse ~ .3f}} under the readout used and {{E65/key_models.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3;readout=raw:apl_effect_rmse ~ .3f}} on raw counts (lower is better; the data's floor is {{data:apl_effect_rmse_floor ~ .3f}}), and an uncalibrated square root gives {{E65/key_models.csv:folder=E44_operating_point;tag=thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_k2_cap3;readout=sqrt:apl_effect_rmse ~ .3f}}. With so little between them, the participation ratio was kept because it measures directly what the cosine weighs and is computed in the same way on the model and on the recordings.

The readout is a static, elementwise map, not a model of the imaging: it has no indicator kinetics and no nuclear localization, and it does not emulate the recordings' per-KC normalization (a z-score of each KC's trace over the whole recording; [the footnote on baseline-noise units](#fn-baseline-noise-units)), which a separate reading of the models does ([the per-KC normalization of the recordings](#per-kc-normalization)).

Below the response criterion the readout holds nothing, where the recordings hold weak and negative values; giving it measurement noise and a calibrated weight for single spikes was tried and leaves the scores where they were ([the next footnote](#fn-readout-low-end)), so it carries neither. Whether the main target is scored on raw counts or through this readout is still to be decided, and until then both are reported; in a model whose KCs have a firing ceiling the two scores nearly coincide ([the firing ceiling for the KCs](#firing-ceiling)).

### How the low end of the readout was tested {#fn-readout-low-end}

**The recordings below the response criterion.** Everything here is computed per recording, from the z-scored value of each KC, odor and trial, and averaged over the recordings of a genotype; a KC × odor entry is a responder when its mean over the three trials is above 1 z and sub-threshold otherwise. For the reproducibility of a band of values, entries are selected by their mean over two of the three trials and read on the third, each trial held out in turn.

For the three terms, a pair's cosine similarity is written as a sum over KCs (the product of the KC's two trial means, divided by the norms of the two odors' response vectors), and each KC's product goes to the term for two responders, for a responder and a sub-threshold entry, or for two sub-threshold entries. The terms add up to the cosine, and a distance is one minus a cosine, so the terms' changes between the control flies and the flies with APL output blocked (TNT) add up to the pair's APL effect.

The intervals come from drawing the recordings of each genotype again with replacement. A term's share of the pattern is its covariance with the whole effect across the 120 pairs divided by the variance of the whole effect, so the three shares add up to 1. The responder × sub-threshold term divides further by its sub-threshold entry: of its {{E68/data_effect_terms.csv:one__effect_mean:observed ~ +.3f}}, {{E68/data_effect_terms.csv:one_weak__effect_mean:observed ~ +.3f}} comes from weakly positive entries, {{E68/data_effect_terms.csv:one_negative__effect_mean:observed ~ +.3f}} from negative ones and {{E68/data_effect_terms.csv:one_unreliable__effect_mean:observed ~ +.3f}} from entries with a trial above 1.5 z, responses that did not repeat.

Part of the sub-threshold structure is a baseline of the KC that also shows in its response to the solvent, part is weak broad tuning, and part of the noise is shared by the trials of one repeat; the negative values in particular depend on how the trial means are made: each KC's trace is z-scored over the whole recording and a trial's response is taken relative to the 5 s before the odor ([the footnote on baseline-noise units](#fn-baseline-noise-units)).

**The two added readings of the recordings.** Beside the four used before (as measured, sub-threshold values set to 0, binarized, corrected for trial-to-trial noise by the correction then in use, which takes the noise of two odors to be independent and is biased: [the flies' variability across the three repeats](#repeat-structure)), the recordings were read with their negative values set to 0 and with every value at or below {{data:kc_noise_floor ~ .2f}} z set to 0. That limit is twice the standard deviation of the noise of a three-trial mean, from the trial-to-trial standard deviation of the control flies' non-responding entries ({{data:ctrl_trial_noise_sd ~ .2f}} z per trial; {{data:tnt_trial_noise_sd ~ .2f}} with APL output blocked (TNT)). Each reading has its own floor of the loss, computed as for the recordings as measured, and a model is always read in the same way as the recordings it is scored against.

**What was added to the model's readout.**

- The readout's values are put in the recordings' units by a factor c, set so that the share of the model's APL-on entries above 1 z is the control flies' response rate.
- The measurement noise is independent Gaussian noise of the control flies' per-trial size on every KC × odor entry, in ten recordings of three trials per model, processed as the recordings are (for the reading as measured, its expected effect on the distances is computed in closed form).
- The one-spike floor is the offset b in (n + b) / (n + b + k) for a KC with at least one spike; 0 stays 0.

k, b and c are found together, by iteration to a fixed point, so that through the noise the model's APL-on entries have the control flies' response rate above 1 z, share between 0.5 and 1.5 z and participation ratio among responders. Nothing from the flies with APL output blocked (TNT), no distance and nothing about the APL effect enters, and the same values are applied to the APL-off counts.

The offset was first to be set on the share between 0.5 and 1 z; that share hardly moves with b once c holds the response rate, the calibration ran to its bounds in most models, and the band was widened. With the wider band it still reaches a bound in part of the saved models (k in {{E68/medians.csv:config=floor_noise;reading=graded:n_K_at_bound ~ .0f}} and b in {{E68/medians.csv:config=floor_noise;reading=graded:n_floor_at_bound ~ .0f}} of the {{E68/medians.csv:config=floor_noise;reading=graded:n ~ .0f}} behind the medians), the reference model and the first joint fit not among them.

Models in which fewer entries hold any spike than the control flies have responders cannot reach the recordings' response rate under any c; these {{E68/medians.csv:config=floor_noise;reading=graded:n_rate_unreachable ~ .0f}}, mostly early models tuned to 5 %, are left out of the medians. A first probe had found the first joint fit's pattern part sensitive to the weight of a single spike; that was with k held fixed, and it disappears once k is calibrated together with the offset. The model's noise is independent for every KC, odor and trial, while part of the recordings' is shared within a repeat and across a KC's odors.

**The membrane-potential terms.** Six models (the reference model, the 70 Hz fit of its family, the first joint fit and the fit of its family with breadth exponent 3, and the best fit so far under each definition from [the APL-effect fits](#apl-effect-fits), which were still running) were simulated again at their fitted parameters, with APL on and with APL removed, with every KC's membrane potential saved; their spike counts equal the saved ones entry for entry. Each KC × odor trace is reduced to its mean over the odor window, relative to the last 100 ms before the odor and as a fraction of the distance to the KC's threshold (its peak in place of the mean gives nearly the same results).

For an entry without a spike the readout adds a weight times the depolarization, at most the reading of one spike; for every non-responding entry (fewer than two spikes) it subtracts a weight times the hyperpolarization. The two weights are set together with k, b and c, on the APL-on run through the noise, so that the model has the control flies' share of entries between 0.25 and 1 z ({{data:ctrl_share_z_025_1 ~ .1%}}) and below −0.25 z ({{data:ctrl_share_z_below_m025 ~ .1%}}).

Three controls separate what the potential holds from what any added term does: each term alone, the potential permuted across the non-spiking KCs within each odor and condition, and the APL-on potential used for both conditions. The terms are a test of where the recordings' low end could come from in the model, not a proposed readout.

### How the pattern part of the APL-effect loss is split into an amplitude part and a shape part, and why no model is chosen by a correlation {#fn-pattern-split}

**What is done.** Each side's per-pair APL effect is taken with its own mean over the 120 pairs removed, and its spread is its standard deviation across the pairs ({{apl_effect/by_variant.csv:folder=E10_joint_fit;tag=k2:spike_counts_cosine__apl_effect_sd_data ~ .3f}} for the flies). The squared pattern part is then exactly the sum of two terms. The amplitude part is the difference between the model's spread and the flies', counted as positive whichever is larger. The shape part is the square root of twice the product of the two spreads times one minus the Pearson correlation r between the two effects: it is zero when the model's effect is the flies' stretched or squeezed about its mean, and it is all of the pattern part when the two spreads are equal. Nothing is fitted and nothing is simulated again: both parts come from the 120 values every model is scored on already.

**How the two parts are read.** They are given with the model's spread as a multiple of the flies' and with Pearson r, because the shape part still grows with the model's spread: of two models with the same r, the one that spreads its effect more widely has the larger shape part as well as the larger amplitude part.

At a given r the pattern part is smallest for a model whose spread is r times the flies', so a low pattern part can come from a spread held below the flies' as well as from a better pattern, and the two parts with the spread say which it is. By the same arithmetic a model does better than an effect with no pattern at all (a pattern part below the flies' spread) only when its spread, as a multiple of the flies', is less than twice its r.

The flies' own spread is not known exactly either: the noise of the recordings adds to it, and it differs between halves of the recordings, so the amplitude part is the least firmly measured of the statistics below. It describes a model and is not a number models are ordered by.

**Why no model is chosen by a correlation.** ρ on the per-pair APL effect and Pearson r leave out the mean and the spread of a model's effect, both of which the loss counts. They are also the less consistent orderings. Every distinct saved model variant was scored, on raw spike counts, against two random halves of the recordings (each genotype split in two), and for each statistic the variants' values against one half were compared with their values against the other, as a Spearman correlation across the variants; one means that the two halves put the models in the same order.

How consistently each statistic orders the saved model variants between two random halves of the recordings (raw spike counts; mean over {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pattern_part:n_splits ~ d}} splits, and the middle 90 % of the splits)

| statistic | agreement between the halves | middle 90 % of the splits |
|---|---|---|
| APL-effect loss | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:loss:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:loss:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:loss:hi ~ .2f}} |
| mean part | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:mean_part:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:mean_part:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:mean_part:hi ~ .2f}} |
| pattern part | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pattern_part:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pattern_part:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pattern_part:hi ~ .2f}} |
| amplitude part | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:amplitude_part:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:amplitude_part:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:amplitude_part:hi ~ .2f}} |
| shape part | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:shape_part:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:shape_part:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:shape_part:hi ~ .2f}} |
| ρ on the per-pair APL effect | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:spearman:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:spearman:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:spearman:hi ~ .2f}} |
| Pearson r on the per-pair APL effect | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pearson:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pearson:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pearson:hi ~ .2f}} |
| pattern part with the pairs weighted by how well the recordings measure them | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pattern_part_w:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pattern_part_w:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pattern_part_w:hi ~ .2f}} |
| per-odor part | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:per_odor_part:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:per_odor_part:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:per_odor_part:hi ~ .2f}} |
| pair-specific part | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pair_specific_part:split_half_rho ~ .2f}} | {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pair_specific_part:lo ~ .2f}} to {{apl_effect_metrics/split_half_reliability.csv:pair_specific_part:hi ~ .2f}} |

The pattern part orders the models more consistently than either correlation, and Pearson r somewhat more consistently than ρ. Among the variants inside the realism bands the order by ρ and the order by the pattern part are only loosely related (a Spearman correlation of {{apl_effect_metrics/metric_correlations_realistic.csv:spearman:pattern_part ~ .2f}} across the variants): the 25 variants with the highest ρ and the 25 with the lowest pattern part have {{apl_effect_metrics/top25_overlap.csv:spearman:pattern_part ~ d}} in common, and ρ's 25 and the 25 with the lowest loss have {{apl_effect_metrics/top25_overlap.csv:spearman:loss ~ d}}. The two parts say where the orders part: the variants with the highest ρ spread their effect well beyond the flies'. The comparison was made on raw spike counts only.

**Weighting the pairs.** A pattern part in which each pair counts by how well the recordings measure it (the inverse of the squared standard error of the pair's effect across the recordings) was compared as well and is not used: it orders the variants inside the realism bands almost as the unweighted one does (a Spearman correlation of {{apl_effect_metrics/metric_correlations_realistic.csv:pattern_part_w:pattern_part ~ .2f}}) and no more consistently between the halves (table).

### How the pattern part of the APL-effect loss is split by odor and by pair {#fn-apl-effect-parts}

**What is done.** A model's pattern error is its per-pair APL effect minus the flies', each with its own mean over the 120 pairs removed first. An additive description over odors gives every odor one term and writes a pair's value as the sum of its two odors' terms, so that an odor contributes the same amount to each of the 15 pairs it is in. Fitted to the pattern error by least squares (16 terms for 120 pairs), it gives the per-odor error, and what it leaves over is the pair-specific error; the per-odor part and the pair-specific part are their root mean squares over the pairs.

The fit is a projection, so the two errors are uncorrelated and their squares add: the squared loss is the squared mean part plus the squared per-odor part plus the squared pair-specific part. The same additive fit applied to an effect itself, the flies' or a model's, gives each odor's share of it, and the fraction of the effect's variance across pairs that the shares explain says how far the effect is a matter of single odors.

**The floors.** They are built as the floor of the loss is: the recordings of each genotype are drawn again with replacement, the resampled effect is scored against the measured one as if it were a model's, and the mean of each part over the draws is its floor, with the middle 90 % of the draws as its interval. Sixteen terms fitted to 120 noisy values take some of the noise with them, and the per-odor floor includes that.

**Why this split.** The two parts point at different kinds of mechanism. An APL that acts too strongly or too weakly on one odor moves all of that odor's pairs together and shows in the per-odor part; an error in which KCs two particular odors have in common shows in the pair-specific part. The assignment is to parts of the error, not to causes: a per-odor part can come from which KCs an odor recruits as well as from how many APL removes, which is what the oracle was built to separate.

**The per-odor APL oracle.** The model has no interaction between odors, so an odor simulated on its own reproduces its column of the 16-odor simulation exactly (checked on the reference model), and each odor can be given an APL of its own.

At the fitted parameters, each odor's ORN input was first scaled until its response fraction with APL off equals that of the flies with APL output blocked (TNT); its APL→KC and APL→bouton scales were then multiplied by one factor, found by bisection on a log scale between 1/16 and 16, until its response fraction with APL on equals the control flies'. It is an [oracle](#fn-oracle): the factors and the input scales are read off the KC data the model is then scored against, and nothing in the circuit is proposed that would set them. Under the calibrated readout the half-saturation k stays the fitted model's, so the readout does not move with the oracle, nor with the breadth exponent in the variants that change it.

### How the firing ceiling works, and how its settings were chosen {#fn-firing-ceiling}

**What is done.** A model KC integrates its input and spikes when its potential crosses its threshold. Before the firing ceiling for the KCs the potential was then reset and integration resumed at once, so that nothing but the input limited how often a KC could fire. Two things were added to the model's KCs, both off unless set, so that every other model on this page is as it was.

- A refractory period: for 3 ms after a spike the potential is held at its reset value and no spike is possible.
- And spike-triggered adaptation: each KC carries a variable that is raised by a fixed increment at each of its spikes and decays back to zero with a time constant, and the KC spikes when its potential exceeds its threshold multiplied by one plus that variable. The increment is thus a fraction of the KC's own threshold and keeps its meaning when the thresholds are re-tuned.

In a run without feedback the ceiling can only remove spikes, and leaves every KC × odor entry of fewer than two spikes as it was; in the full model the response rates shift a little through APL and the KC–KC inhibition, and at every setting both were brought back to the base model's own by two re-tunings in turn: the somatic threshold on the response rate with APL off, then one common factor on the APL→KC and APL→bouton scales on the response rate with APL on, the KC–KC scale left as fitted.

**The time constant and the strength.** With a time constant of 1 s, twice the length of the odor, the adaptation hardly decays within a response: every spike makes the next one harder, and the ceiling is a budget of spikes per odor more than a limit on the firing rate. The time constant matters more than the strength. On the current reference model three strengths were run at time constants of 50 ms, 200 ms and 1 s, each at fixed scales with both response rates held.

At 50 ms the adaptation recovers within the odor and the APL-effect loss on raw counts stays between {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a3_t50:apl_raw_rmse ~ .3f}} and {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a1_t50:apl_raw_rmse ~ .3f}}, from {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_base:apl_raw_rmse ~ .3f}} without a ceiling (lower is better; floor {{data:apl_effect_rmse_floor ~ .3f}}); at 200 ms it is between {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a3_t200:apl_raw_rmse ~ .3f}} and {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a1_t200:apl_raw_rmse ~ .3f}}, and at 1 s between {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a2_t1000:apl_raw_rmse ~ .3f}} and {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a1_t1000:apl_raw_rmse ~ .3f}}. The refractory period alone leaves it at {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3:apl_raw_rmse ~ .3f}}. The three strengths were set in a pilot on the reference model with APL off, at the 1 s time constant, so that its largest spike count comes to about 40, 20 and 10: increments of {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a1_t1000:kc_adapt_inc ~ .3f}}, {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a2_t1000:kc_adapt_inc ~ .3f}} and {{E69/stats_variants.csv:ref40_r3_a3_t1000:kc_adapt_inc ~ .3f}} of the threshold per spike.

**The two settings that were fitted.** The literature gives no largest spike count for a KC, only means and standard deviations per response: {{lit:4.9 ± 3.0 # spikes per response of α′/β′ KCs to a 500 ms odor (mean ± standard deviation, whole-cell recordings, APL intact), Turner, Bazhenov and Laurent (2008), as quoted in E69_kc_firing_ceiling.md, Design (part B), Realism and Caveats}} spikes for α′/β′ KCs and {{lit:2.2 ± 1.2 # spikes per response of α/β KCs to a 500 ms odor (mean ± standard deviation, whole-cell recordings, APL intact), Turner, Bazhenov and Laurent (2008), as quoted in E69_kc_firing_ceiling.md, Realism and Caveats}} for α/β KCs in whole-cell recordings with a 0.5 s odor (Turner, Bazhenov and Laurent, 2008; other odors and concentrations than the KC data's, APL intact). The bound used is the mean plus three standard deviations of the α′/β′ KCs, about {{lit:14 # the bound on a KC's spike count to one odor with APL on that the firing ceiling for the KCs takes from whole-cell recordings: the mean plus three standard deviations (4.9 + 3 x 3.0 = 13.9) of the spikes per response of α′/β′ KCs to a 500 ms odor in Turner, Bazhenov and Laurent (2008); E69_kc_firing_ceiling.md, Design (part B) and Caveats}} spikes, a reading that a measured largest count would replace. The literature setting is the weakest of the three strengths, at which the largest count of the breadth-2 APL-effect fit with APL on ({{E69/stats_variants.csv:e67cal_r3_a1_t1000:max_count_on ~ .0f}} at fixed scales, {{E69/stats_variants.csv:rate0.068_aplboth_refr3_adapt0.04142t1000_k2:max_count_on ~ .0f}} once fitted) is nearest that bound.

The stronger setting is the middle strength, the weakest at which the half-saturation of [the calibrated readout](#fn-calibrated-readout) runs to the upper end of its range for that fit: the model's counts with APL on are then no more concentrated than the control flies' responses, the readout has nothing to compress, and the two definitions of the model's side give the same scores. There the largest count of the breadth-2 fit with APL on is {{E69/stats_variants.csv:rate0.068_aplboth_refr3_adapt0.1114t1000_k2:max_count_on ~ .0f}} spikes and the 99th percentile of its responders' counts {{E69/stats_variants.csv:rate0.068_aplboth_refr3_adapt0.1114t1000_k2:p99_resp_count_on ~ .0f}}, about the mean of the α′/β′ KCs in the recordings, so the setting allows those KCs less than they show; in the reference model, whose counts are higher, the same strength gives a largest count of {{E69/stats_variants.csv:thr40_gain1.5_rate0.068_aplboth_refr3_adapt0.1114t1000_k2:max_count_on ~ .0f}}.

Each fit is the joint fit under the APL-effect loss with the term on raw counts and the term under the calibrated readout at equal weight, the response rates held as constraints at the flies' response rate, the ceiling fixed and the usual four parameters free (the somatic threshold, the APL→KC scale with the KC→APL scale tied to it, the APL→bouton scale up to three times the baseline's, and the KC–KC scale), started from the run of its setting at fixed scales.

For the breadth-2 family the fit without a ceiling is that family's fit with both definitions in the loss, which had ended at practically the same model as its fit under the readout, the one in the best-models table. Every fit simulated again at its fitted parameters reproduces its saved spike counts exactly.

**What the ceiling is not.** One adaptation variable per KC with one time constant is the simplest form that bounds a count. Real KC adaptation has several time scales (calcium-activated potassium currents, synaptic depression at the claws), and a time constant longer than the odor makes the model's version close to a cap on the number of spikes per odor.

The result needs that: at the flies' 2 s pulse the 1 s adaptation wears off within the odor and about a fifth of the level on raw counts is lost, with the indicator's kinetics as measured in the recordings ([the time course of the APL effect in the flies' traces](#trace-time-course)), and it returns with an adaptation of 3 s ([the flies' recording protocol in the model](#flies-protocol)). Whether it holds with a less schematic adaptation has not been tested. The strength stays a choice until the largest spike count of a fly KC to a 0.5 s odor is measured.

### What "baseline-noise units" are, and the response criterion of the realism bands {#fn-baseline-noise-units}

**What the baseline noise of a KC is.** A KC's signal in a recording is its fluorescence trace with 0.7 times the fluorescence of the neuropil around it subtracted, neither detrended nor divided by a resting fluorescence. A recording holds 51 odor presentations (the 16 odors and the solvent, three times each), and in the 5 s before each of them no odor is present. The baseline noise of a KC is the standard deviation of its signal within those 51 pre-odor windows, taken after each window's own mean is subtracted from its values and pooled over the windows (the summed squares divided by the number of values less the 51 means removed).

Subtracting each window's mean keeps the slow drift of the trace over the {{lit:40 # about 7,194 imaging volumes at 2.96 volumes per second, 40.5 minutes per recording: notes/yang_response_normalization/recordings.csv, columns n_volumes and volume_rate}} minutes of a recording out of it, and the windows hold no odor response, so what is left is how much the KC's signal fluctuates from one imaging volume to another when nothing is presented: its measurement noise. It is one number per KC, computed from the raw traces for every KC of the {{data:n_recordings_ctrl ~ .0f}} recordings of control flies and the {{data:n_recordings_tnt ~ .0f}} recordings with APL output blocked (TNT).

**A response in baseline-noise units.** A trial's response is the mean of the KC's signal from 2 to 8 s after odor onset minus its mean over the 5 s before, and the response to an odor is the mean over the odor's three trials, the same windows and the same mean as in the recordings' own analysis. Divided by the KC's baseline noise, it is the response in baseline-noise units: by how many times its own noise the KC's signal rose.

The recordings' own values, the ones used everywhere else on this page, are the same differences divided by something else, the standard deviation of the KC's signal over the whole recording (a z-score of the whole trace). A response in baseline-noise units is therefore also the z-scored response multiplied by the ratio of the KC's whole-trace standard deviation to its baseline noise. Recomputed from the raw traces, the z-scored traces and the per-trial responses agree with those saved with the recordings, and with the values this page uses, to the rounding of the stored numbers in every recording.

**Why the recordings' own unit is not a fixed one.** One z is the standard deviation of a KC's signal over its whole recording, which holds the KC's noise, its slow drift and its own odor responses. The unit is therefore larger in a KC that responds to more odors, or more strongly: the median ratio of the whole-trace standard deviation to the baseline noise is {{data:kc_scale_ratio_0 ~ .1f}} for the KCs that respond to none of the 16 odors, {{data:kc_scale_ratio_1 ~ .1f}} for those that respond to one, {{data:kc_scale_ratio_3 ~ .1f}} to three, {{data:kc_scale_ratio_6 ~ .1f}} to six, {{data:kc_scale_ratio_8 ~ .1f}} to eight and {{data:kc_scale_ratio_11plus ~ .1f}} to eleven or more (both genotypes together, the number of odors counted by the recordings' criterion).

The recordings' criterion for a response, a three-trial mean above 1 z, is thus relative to each KC: the same change in fluorescence over the same noise counts as a response in a KC that responds to little else and not in one that responds to many odors. A model KC's criterion, two or more spikes to the odor, does not depend on what else the KC does.

**The threshold.** In baseline-noise units one threshold serves every KC of every recording: a response is a three-trial mean above {{data:noise_threshold ~ .2f}} times the KC's baseline noise. That value is the one at which the control flies' response rate (the share of KC × odor entries that respond, averaged over the recordings) equals their response rate by the recordings' own criterion, {{data:ctrl_frac ~ .3f}}; it was found on the control recordings alone and is applied unchanged to the recordings with APL output blocked (TNT).

The two criteria coincide for a KC whose whole-trace standard deviation is that many times its baseline noise, about the median of the KCs that respond to three or four odors ({{data:kc_scale_ratio_3 ~ .2f}} and {{data:kc_scale_ratio_4 ~ .2f}}); for a KC below that ratio the criterion in baseline-noise units is the stricter of the two, for a KC above it the more lenient. The threshold is a calibration and not a significance level: the baseline noise is the fluctuation of single imaging volumes, whereas a response is a difference between two window means averaged over three trials.

**How the realism bands use it.** Since 2026-11-10 all four bands count a response in a model as two or more spikes to the odor, as before, and a response in the flies as a three-trial mean above the threshold in baseline-noise units. Each side then has a criterion that is the same for all of its KCs, and the two are tied at one point: the threshold holds the control flies at their measured response rate, and the models are tuned to their response rate with APL on by the two-spike count.

The band on the response rate with APL on thus tests a model's own firing, and the other three compare what follows from it on each side: how many more responses there are without APL (the ratio of the response rates), which odors have them (response rate ρ, against the control flies' per-odor response rates counted in baseline-noise units) and how they are spread over the KCs (the distances between the distributions of odors per KC, with APL on against the control flies and with APL off against the flies with APL output blocked (TNT), the band being the most atypical recording's distance from the other recordings of its genotype, all counted in baseline-noise units).

The limits of the three bands on the response rates are as they were. No model was simulated again: the change is on the flies' side, and each saved model was scored again from its saved responses.

**Why not the recordings' own criterion on the flies' side.** Until 2026-11-10 the bands compared the models' two-spike responses with the flies' responses above 1 z: a fixed criterion against one that grows with how much a KC responds. The difference between the two criteria is of the size the band on odors per KC is meant to detect.

Counted by the two criteria, the same flies' distributions of odors per KC are {{data:noise_ctrl_odors_per_kc_tv_vs_z ~ .3f}} apart in control flies and {{data:noise_tnt_odors_per_kc_tv_vs_z ~ .3f}} with APL output blocked (TNT) (the distance of the main text, half the summed absolute differences between the five shares), against bands of {{data:ctrl_odors_per_kc_tv_max ~ .3f}} and {{data:tnt_odors_per_kc_tv_max ~ .3f}} by that criterion: a model with exactly the flies' distribution in fixed units would have used up about two fifths of the band before any error of its own.

The z-score makes the criterion more lenient for KCs that respond to little and stricter for KCs that respond to much, so by it fewer KCs are silent and fewer respond to eight or more odors (table below), and a model was held to a distribution with both ends drawn in. The current reference model was outside the band with APL off by that criterion and is inside it by the present one.

**Why not put the models through the recordings' normalization instead.** The other way of comparing like with like is to read each model as the recordings were made (the per-KC reading, [the per-KC normalization of the recordings](#per-kc-normalization)): each model KC's spike counts are placed in a simulated recording with the recordings' trial structure, noise and drift, the trace is z-scored over the whole session, and a response is a value above 1 z. That keeps the flies' values as measured, but the simulated noise has a level that must be set, and it is set, for each model, so that the model's response rate with APL on is the control flies'. The band on that response rate can then not fail, whatever the model's firing.

A fit whose response rates were counted through this reading weakened its APL and KC-KC inhibition, its somatic threshold hardly moving, until {{apl_effect/by_variant.csv:folder=E74_apl_effect_by_odors_per_kc;tag=zcaplrate_rate0.068_aplzcell_refr3_adapt0.04142t1000_thrin0.25_k2:rate_on ~ .3f}} of its KC × odor entries held two or more spikes with APL on, against the flies' {{data:ctrl_frac ~ .3f}} and the band's upper limit of 0.085, and was inside all four bands as read. The reading also enlarges a broadly responding model KC's unit less than the recordings enlarge a fly KC's, so part of the mismatch stays, and its verdicts shift with its settings. It is kept as a second description of a model, reported beside the bands where a model has been read that way; it does not decide them, and fits hold their response rates on the two-spike count.

The KC data under the two response criteria (means over the recordings of a genotype; a cell with two values gives control flies / APL output blocked (TNT))
